paragraphs.text: English translation of the verified source: “He made the letter lamed king over intercourse, bound a crown to it, joined them together, and formed with them Libra in the world, Tishrei in the year, and the gallbladder in the person, male and female. He made the letter nun king over scent, bound a crown to it, joined them together, and formed with them Scorpio in the world, Cheshvan in the year, and the intestines in the person, male and female. He made the letter samekh king over sleep, bound a crown to it, joined them together, and formed with them Sagittarius in the world, Kislev in the year, and the stomach in the person, male and female.”

paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “I am [Anochi]”: at that moment the sanctuary was purified; the alien power did not draw near, and the sanctuary shone by itself, because the evil inclination was then nullified from the world. The Holy One, blessed be He, was exalted in His glory alone. Thus it was said, “I am Hashem your God.” This is a complete mystery contained in the holy Name. Aleph: to unite the mystery of the holy Name in its levels, to make it one, for its mystery is vav. Nun: the mystery of fearing the Holy One, blessed be He, and knowing that there is judgment and a Judge; that there is a good reward for the righteous and punishment for the wicked; for the mystery of this letter is the lower hei.”

paragraphs.text: Textual context and editorial distinction:  This passage interprets the nun within the letters of Anochi, not as a standalone discussion of Cheshvan. Rav Tzadok connects its identification with awe, divine judgment and the lower hei to the letter governing the month. The translated passage includes the preceding contrast between holy revelation and the displaced evil inclination.

paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “It was taught: There are two letters of this kind; just as we explained with the letter vav, so it is with nun. Although the matter has already been established, nun is expounded as follows. The bent nun: this is the Matronita [the Shechinah]. Alongside her stands vav, which is Yesod, so that she may be blessed through it. The straight nun signifies the extension of Tiferes. The letters are thus incorporated and united with one another. And if you ask: Why does vav turn away its face from the bent nun and turn its face toward the straight nun? ...”

rich.text: English translation of verified source:

“It was taught: There are two letters of this kind; just as we explained with the letter vav, so it is with nun. Although the matter has already been established, nun is expounded as follows. The bent nun: this is the Matronita [the Shechinah]. Alongside her stands vav, which is Yesod, so that she may be blessed through it. The straight nun signifies the extension of Tiferes. The letters are thus incorporated and united with one another. And if you ask: Why does vav turn away its face from the bent nun and turn its face toward the straight nun? ...”

paragraphs.text: Textual context and editorial distinction:  The bent nun is explicitly identified with the Matronita and linked to Yesod; the straight nun corresponds to an extension of Tiferes. This supports Rav Tzadok’s association of the lower hei with Malchus. The verse “A king establishes the land through justice” and the ensuing application to Cheshvan belong to Rav Tzadok’s own argument, not to the quoted Zohar lines. The final question above begins a further discussion not reproduced here.

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Divrei Soferim 13, paragraph 1, phrase window 9–16: “… therefore one's fear of sin must precede his wisdom, as stated in Avot, for otherwise it cannot endure, and "if there is no fear, there is no wisdom." And this explains why the Talmud in Shabbat first likened it to outer keys, and then conversely likened fear to the inner courtyard and Torah to the outer gate, which appears contradictory—presenting fear as inner and Torah as the entryway—alongside the mishnaic dictum in Avot: "If there is no wisdom, there is no fear." But in truth, the fear of Hashem is itself wisdom, as stated in Devarim Rabbah [11]: "By your lives, all wisdom and the entire Torah are a single simple matter: whoever fears Me and performs words of Torah has all wisdom and the entire Torah in his heart; from where is this derived...", and this represents Lower Wisdom (Chochmah Tata'ah), the wisdom of Solomon of whom it is said, "And he was wiser than all men," which is the pinnacle of human intellect, attained in this world solely through the fear implanted in the heart. Therefore, concerning one who possesses Torah but lacks the fear of Heaven, they expounded in Yoma [72b] upon the verse "the purchase price to buy wisdom," that his Torah is merely considered currency to purchase wisdom, for the core of wisdom is the direct awareness that there is a Creator, through which awe falls upon him naturally, and from this vantage Torah is termed the entrance-gate; and thus the Sanhedrin are called "those who sit at the gate," translated in the Aramaic Targum on "to the gate" as "to the gate of the Beit Din," which serves as the gate to the courtyard and the gate unto Hashem, …”

paragraphs.text: English translation of the verified source: “‘The Lord God caused a deep sleep [to fall upon the man].’ Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin in the name of Rabbi Levi said: ‘Sleep is the beginning of decline: he sleeps and does not toil in Torah, and does not attend to his work.’ Rav said: ‘There are three kinds of deep sleep: the sleep of ordinary slumber, the sleep of prophecy, and the sleep of collapse.’ The Rabbis added a sleep of folly; and Rabbi Chanina bar Yitzchak taught that sleep is a lesser reflection of death, a dream of prophecy, and Shabbos of the World to Come.”

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Resisei Layla 51, paragraph 3: “This is also why the years of Creation are counted from Tishrei, corresponding to the level of primordial thought according to which Israel sanctifies the times. Thus the lunar conjunctions, which determine the lunar months, are calculated from the traditional epoch of BeHaRaD, following the view that the world was created in Tishrei, as is known from the calculations of intercalation. The solar seasons, however, are counted from Nisan, because that is when Creation became manifest in the realm of action: the moon receives from the sun, and the power of the sun becomes operative. Israel were given that month in order to sanctify the moon. In primordial thought the moon too was a great light, as it will again be in the future, when from the perspective of that thought the two luminaries are both great. Only in the realm of action was the moon diminished, because in this world “one who eats what is not his own is ashamed.” Awe is itself identified with this holy shame, and this is the quality of Israel—who are characterized by bashfulness—which is absent from the nations. Through this very diminishment, Israel sanctify the appointed times. In the Oral Torah the central sanctification is therefore fixed in Tishrei, on Rosh Hashanah, for Israel’s unique power is that their sanctity can reach all the way to the root of Divine thought. They therefore count the lunar year from Tishrei, corresponding to the thought in which both luminaries are great. This is the entire wisdom of the sages of Israel in the Oral Torah: to cleave to His wisdom and His thought, through which their own wisdom itself becomes Torah. This is not so with the sages of the nations. Their wisdom can recognize that one thing is evil and another good, but they believe that evil, once present, has no rectification; such is the conclusion of unaided wisdom. Thus the Midrash teaches that when Wisdom was asked what should happen to the sinner, it answered, “Evil pursues sinners.” Therefore they count the Flood from Nisan. According to their understanding, even under strict justice there could have been no alternative to the Flood, for sin necessarily draws punishment after it. They believe that a being cannot truly change from what it is. Thus Balaam did not change even though he knew that his path represented the ultimate evil.”

Through this very diminishment, Israel sanctify the appointed times. In the Oral Torah the central sanctification is therefore fixed in Tishrei, on Rosh Hashanah, for Israel’s unique power is that their sanctity can reach all the way to the root of Divine thought. They therefore count the lunar year from Tishrei, corresponding to the thought in which both luminaries are great. This is the entire wisdom of the sages of Israel in the Oral Torah: to cleave to His wisdom and His thought, through which their own wisdom itself becomes Torah. This is not so with the sages of the nations. Their wisdom can recognize that one thing is evil and another good, but they believe that evil, once present, has no rectification; such is the conclusion of unaided wisdom. Thus the Midrash teaches that when Wisdom was asked what should happen to the sinner, it answered, “Evil pursues sinners.” Therefore they count the Flood from Nisan. According to their understanding, even under strict justice there could have been no alternative to the Flood, for sin necessarily draws punishment after it. They believe that a being cannot truly change from what it is. Thus Balaam did not change even though he knew that his path represented the ultimate evil.”

paragraphs.text: English translation of the verified source: Rashi (on “And these follow their respective views”): “For Rabbi Eliezer, the world was created in Tishrei, for the counting of the generations begins from Tishrei; accordingly the Flood must have begun in Marcheshvan and lasted twelve months. paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “Our Sages further expounded another mystery: ‘The generation that departs is the generation that comes’; one who went lame returns lame, and one who went blind returns blind. They also taught that Moshe was destined to receive the Torah in the generation of the Flood; but because they were wicked, Scripture states, ‘For he too is flesh’ (be-shagam hu basar). ‘Be-shagam’ is Moshe. Why does it call him ‘be-shagam’? Rather, Koheles concealed the matter by omitting the letter beis from ‘be-shagam’: ‘I said that this too (she-gam) is vanity.’”

paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “When the vav is completed within ten, six times, it amounts to sixty, in order to raise [them] from the dust. At every sixty-year interval within that sixth millennium, the hei grows stronger and ascends by its degrees. And in the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above and the springs of wisdom below will open, and the world will be prepared to enter the seventh [millennium], like a person who prepares on the sixth day, as the sun sets, to enter Shabbos. The sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noach’s life ... all the fountains of the great deep burst open’ (Genesis 7:11).”

Rav Tzadok interprets the springs below as Oral Torah and the gates above as supernal revelation. The distinction is his application of the Zoharic imagery, not an additional sentence supplied in this passage.

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Resisei Layla 48, paragraph 3, phrase window 1–8: “On the fourth day He created the sun and the moon, and in the future He will exact punishment from those who worship them. The creation of the luminaries to illuminate the world parallels the giving of the Torah, which shone the light of Torah upon all who enter the world. Our Sages of blessed memory taught (Shabbat 89b) that Mount Sinai was so named because hatred descended there upon the idolatrous nations, through the attribute of victory, the level of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, whose face was like the face of the sun (Bava Batra 75a). Our Sages of blessed memory also taught (Nedarim 8b) that in the future there will be no Gehinnom; rather, the sun will be removed from its sheath—the righteous, etc., and the wicked, etc. This follows the principle: 'The righteous shall walk in them, while sinners shall stumble in them.' Likewise, they taught (Shabbat 88b) that for those who turn to the left in Torah it becomes a potion of death; 'evil pursues sinners,' for the sin itself becomes the punishment. This is the meaning of the statement (Bava Batra 16a): he is the evil inclination; he is the Angel of Death.”

paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “Two thousand years of chaos: ‘The earth was chaos’; two thousand years of Torah: ‘The spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters’—and ‘water’ means nothing other than Torah. ‘The face of the waters’ refers to its two aspects, positive and negative commandments, white and red, right and left. Then come the two thousand years of the days of Mashiach: ‘God said: Let there be light, and there was light.’ ... ‘Let there be light’ is Pesach, the light of the fourteenth; ‘and there was light’ is Rosh Hashanah, of which it is said, ‘And there was a day.’ Here ‘and there was,’ and there ‘and there was’; wherever ‘and there was’ occurs it conveys a language of distress.”

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Resisei Layla 31, paragraph 1: “The Torah rescues a person from illusions, and as it is written in Avot DeRabbi Natan (beginning of Chapter 20): "Whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him stray thoughts of, etc.," and as it is written (Proverbs 6:22): "When you walk it shall lead you; when you lie down it shall watch over you; and when you awake it shall converse with you." The explanation is that the imaginative faculty (ha-medameh) overpowers in three ways: The first: when he is occupied in affairs of this physical world which is entirely an illusion, wherein he must be cautious not to drown in its illusions, Heaven forbid, and engage only in that which is truly necessary for his upkeep.”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin —  Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 3 — paragraph 7, source phrases 7:1–9:end.Extended English quotation from Akiva interlinear: as taught in the Holy Zohar (Beshalach 44a) : It is the customary way of the world that when a person rises from his bed, the sheet he slept upon emits an unrefined, repulsive odor; but when Elisha arose, the sheet emitted a fragrance like the Garden of Eden. paragraphs.text: English translation of the verified source: “From the time Rabbi Meir died, the composers of parables ceased ... Purity took away taste and fragrance.” Rav Huna found a fragrant date, took it, and wrapped it in his cloth. Rabbah his son came and said: “I smell the fragrance of the [fragrant] date.” Rav Huna said: “My son, there is purity in you,” and gave it to him. Meanwhile, his grandson Abba arrived; Rabbah took it and gave it to him. Rav Huna said: “My son, you have gladdened my heart and set my teeth on edge.”

paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “There remained another Shabbos that had not been mentioned, and it stood in longing. It said before Him: ‘Master of the world, from the day You made me I have been called Shabbos, but no day exists without a night.’ He said to her: ‘My daughter, you are Shabbos and I call you Shabbos; but I shall crown you with an even higher crown.’ A proclamation went forth: ‘You shall revere My sanctuary’—this is the Shabbos of Friday evening, which is awe, and awe dwells within her. And who is He? It is the Holy One, blessed be He, Who includes all and says, ‘I am Hashem.’ ... ‘My Shabboses’ signifies the encompassing circle and the inner square; they are two, corresponding to two sanctifications mentioned by us.”

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Divrei Soferim 13, paragraph 1, phrase window 9–16: “… therefore one's fear of sin must precede his wisdom, as stated in Avot, for otherwise it cannot endure, and "if there is no fear, there is no wisdom." And this explains why the Talmud in Shabbat first likened it to outer keys, and then conversely likened fear to the inner courtyard and Torah to the outer gate, which appears contradictory—presenting fear as inner and Torah as the entryway—alongside the mishnaic dictum in Avot: "If there is no wisdom, there is no fear." But in truth, the fear of Hashem is itself wisdom, as stated in Devarim Rabbah [11]: "By your lives, all wisdom and the entire Torah are a single simple matter: whoever fears Me and performs words of Torah has all wisdom and the entire Torah in his heart; from where is this derived...", and this represents Lower Wisdom (Chochmah Tata'ah), the wisdom of Solomon of whom it is said, "And he was wiser than all men," which is the pinnacle of human intellect, attained in this world solely through the fear implanted in the heart. Therefore, concerning one who possesses Torah but lacks the fear of Heaven, they expounded in Yoma [72b] upon the verse "the purchase price to buy wisdom," that his Torah is merely considered currency to purchase wisdom, for the core of wisdom is the direct awareness that there is a Creator, through which awe falls upon him naturally, and from this vantage Torah is termed the entrance-gate; and thus the Sanhedrin are called "those who sit at the gate," translated in the Aramaic Targum on "to the gate" as "to the gate of the Beit Din," which serves as the gate to the courtyard and the gate unto Hashem, …”

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 115, paragraph 1, phrase window 1–8: “When a person innovates an insight in the Torah, it must not stem from any personal bias in the heart that desires it to be so, nor for self-aggrandizement, nor to dispute the words of another, or the like; but solely from the pure yearning to know the Truth. And then, even if he errs, it is termed words of Torah and the words of the living God, for behold, the Talmud explicitly records the words of those who erred and opinions that were rejected from practical halakhah, showing that even the initial hypothesis (hava amina) is words of Torah; for thus the Blessed Name established the process: first an initial conception, and only subsequently arriving at the truth; and that initial conception is likewise from the Blessed Name and constitutes the words of the living God. But when it stems from personal bias, then it is not termed words of Torah at all; as written concerning Jeroboam: "the month which he had devised of his own heart" (I Kings 12:33), and certainly he expounded to them some textual exegesis and derivation that the Harvest Festival falls in Marcheshvan; …”

paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “We have learned that wherever this serpent goes it follows the mystery of the ‘Woman of Valor,’ and the ‘Woman of Harlotry’ seeks to arrange herself in the same form, but cannot. The mark and letter belonging to the Woman of Valor is the letter hei, and so it is fitting for her. The Woman of Harlotry has a mark and letter resembling the proper form, but it cannot be established as such; her letter is kuf. It is fashioned in imitation of hei, like an ape among human beings that imitates human beings but cannot truly become the same. Moshe made that serpent according to the mark appropriate to it; it was perpetually arranged to do harm. Through it Adam sinned and was expelled from Gan Eden, his dwelling place resembling the dwelling above.”

Rav Tzadok applies this imagery to distorted appetite and the potential for desire to be redirected toward Torah. The translation reflects the passage’s main continuous argument without presenting the marginal textual variants as part of the quotation. The author’s older folio reference (II 148b) should be compared with the segmentation and Vilna-page markers of the available digital Zohar text; the verified passage is linked by its digital location, Terumah 36:413.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Rav Tzadok —  Tzidkat HaTzadik 242 — paragraph 1, phrase 41–49.Extended English quotation from Akiva interlinear: However, through fear and fence-building it is impossible to subjugate and nullify them completely; for wasting seed is an actual soul-faculty, since from it could have been born a living human soul, and therefore it assuredly contains of his vitality. And the vitality of a Jew contains complete holiness derived from the portion of Hashem inherited from the Patriarchs which he bequeaths to his offspring, and of this sanctity is also present within that seminal drop; only that it was enclothed in the lustful thought and desire of the evil inclination overpowering him during the act and in the action-garment of the completed physical deed.Connection (editorial): Contextual connection (editorial): Both passages address the proper use and refinement of human desire. This is a thematic comparison; the added passage should be understood in its own setting, and is not represented as Rav Tzadok’s direct proof-text.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin —  Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 18 — paragraph 14, source phrases 14:1–17:end.Extended English quotation from Akiva interlinear: meaning that regarding Shabbat as well, had it embodied the absolute divine Will directly without mediation, Shabbat could never be overridden for the preservation of life (pikuach nefesh)—for how could saving a life supersede the supreme divine Will? paragraphs.text: English translation of verified source:  “Rabbi Yitzchak son of Rabbi Yose was coming from Cappadocia to Lod, when he met Rabbi Yehudah. Rabbi Yitzchak asked whether the Sages had considered that the evil inclination would one day vanish from the world except at the time needed for union. [Rabbi Yehudah] said to him: ‘By your life, the evil inclination will be needed in the world just as rain is needed in the world; for were it not for the evil inclination, there would be no joy in the discussion of Torah. Yet it would no longer be foul as formerly, leading one to sin. This is the meaning of: “They shall not do harm or destroy on all My holy mountain.”’ Rabbi Shimon said: ‘It is the heart, in which the evil inclination dwells.’ Rabbi Eliezer said: ‘A good heart is the building of body and soul’; hence it is written, ‘You shall love Hashem your God with all your heart.’”

paragraphs.text: Textual context and editorial distinction:  The striking “joy in Torah discussion” formula is present word-for-word in this digital passage and provides an independently verified source. However, its electronic segmentation is Zohar, Toldot 6:57 (the source includes a Vilna-page overlay of 138a), whereas Rav Tzadok names Midrash HaNe’elam, Zohar I 131a. That folio discrepancy has NOT been resolved; both identifications are recorded, and the digital passage is not silently passed off as an exact match to the older page number.

paragraphs.text: Additional Kisvei Rav Tzadok parallel — Tzidkat HaTzadik 242, paragraph 1, phrase window 9–16: “… drawing him toward the study hall and words of Torah, wherein the evil inclination becomes 'very good', as written in the Midrash HaNe'elam (Zohar Part I, 138a), that the deep desire for Torah is fueled through it. And this applies to the future; and so too regarding the past, when one is overwhelmed by love of Hashem and Hashem reciprocates toward him: he realizes that 'all our works You have wrought for us' entirely for our benefit, …”

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Ishbitz–Radzin —  Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 6 — paragraph 44, source phrases 44:1–46:end.Extended English quotation from Akiva interlinear: And as taught in the Midrash HaNe'elam in Zohar Chadash (Bereishit 28b): Scripture should have formulated it “and it was so”; however, concerning anything that perpetually requires ongoing divine assistance, “and it was so” is not stated; examine there, for regarding whatever is destined to continually increase, “and it was so” is omitted (and see below, section 46).
